query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor copper doping (~5 at%) into a baseline high-entropy alloy (e.g., an AlCoCrFeNi-type system) will create enhanced thermal conduction pathways, thereby improving the heat-transfer capability of intermediate layers in plasma-facing reactor components while maintaining sufficient structural integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy intermediate layer (predominantly FCC and/or BCC phases) currently used in plasma-facing reactor components that exhibits acceptable mechanical strength and microstructural stability but limited heat-transfer efficiency.
generation.intervention: Alter the alloy composition via the controlled addition of approximately 5 at% Cu during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Under high-temperature service conditions typical of plasma-facing reactor environments (approximately 700–1000 °C) and during cyclic thermal loading.
generation.structural_mediator: A homogeneous microstructure where the added Cu is uniformly dispersed, forming conductive paths without inducing significant phase segregation or grain-boundary embrittlement.
generation.mechanism: Copper possesses high intrinsic thermal conductivity. When added in small amounts, Cu is expected to create interconnected conductive channels that enhance phonon and electron transport while the overall multiphase structure of the alloy maintains its load-bearing and creep-resistant properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped HEA, the Cu-doped alloy will exhibit an improved heat-transfer capability (i.e., higher effective thermal conductivity) without a significant compromise in tensile strength or creep resistance, compared with current intermediate-layer performance.
generation.baseline: The performance characteristics of existing HEA intermediate layers lacking Cu doping under similar high-temperature and thermal cycling conditions.
generation.boundary: If the Cu concentration exceeds the optimal level or if processing conditions lead to excessive phase separation, the alloy may develop deleterious microstructural features that compromise structural integrity.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the thermal conductivity improvement and the long-term effects on mechanical properties under cyclic thermal loading are uncertain and must be quantified experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA intermediate-layer samples using identical processing routes: one set with ~5 at% Cu doping and one set without (the control). Subject them to simulated plasma-facing reactor conditions including high temperatures (700–1000 °C) and thermal cycling. Characterize their microstructures via SEM and XRD.
measurements: Thermal conductivity measurements at the target temperature range
Tensile strength and creep resistance under elevated temperatures
Microstructural analysis to assess phase homogeneity and stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-doped samples do not display a statistically significant increase (e.g., at least ~10% improvement) in thermal conductivity compared to the control, or if mechanical properties (tensile strength or creep resistance) degrade by more than ~10%, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Synthesis of High-Entropy Alloys with a Tailored Composition and Phase Structure Using a Single Configurable Target

Abstract: AbstractPreviously, refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with high crystallinity were synthesized using a configurable target without heat treatment. This study builds upon prior investigations to develop nonrefractory elemental HEAs with low crystallinity using a novel target system. Different targets with various elemental compositions, i.e., Co20Cr20Ni20Mn20Mo20 (target 1), Co30Cr15Ni25Mn15Mo15 (target 2), and Co15Cr25Cu20Mn20Ni20 (target 3), are designed to modify the phase structure. The elemental composition is varied to ensure face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) phase stabilization. In target 1, the FCC and BCC phases coexist, whereas targets 2 and 3 are characterized by a single FCC phase. Thin films based on targets 1 and 2 exhibit crystalline phases followed by annealing, as indicated by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analyses. Fabrication of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Coating on an AISI 304 Substrate via a CoFe2Ni Intermediate Layer

Abstract: Through laser metal deposition, attempts were made to coat AlCoCrFeNi, a high-entropy alloy (HEA), on an AISI 304 stainless steel substrate to integrate their properties. However, the direct coating of the AlCoCrFeNi HEA on the AISI 304 substrate was found to be unviable due to cracks at the interface between these two materials. The difference in compositional change was suspected to be the source of the cracks. Therefore, a new transition route was performed by coating an intermediate layer of CoFe2Ni on the AISI 304 substrate. Investigations into the microstructure, phase composition, elemental composition and Vickers hardness were carried out in this study. Consistent metallurgical bonding was observed along both of the interfaces. It was found that the AlCoCrFeNi alloy solidified into a dendritic microstructure. The X-ray diffraction pattern revealed a transition of the crystal structure of the AISI 304 substrate to the AlCoCrFeNi HEA.
